pointers.sentence: A field may have a default that the database applies, `db_default=` (5.0), beside the `default=` that Django applies to a new instance (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field._get_default`).

A new instance given no value holds a `DatabaseDefault` in the value's place, unless the field also has `default=`, and the insert leaves the column out where it can, or writes `"DEFAULT"` or the default's expression (`django/db/models/sql/compiler.py:SQLInsertCompiler.as_sql`, `django/db/models/expressions.py:DatabaseDefault`).

A new instance given no value holds a `DatabaseDefault` in the value's place, unless the field also has `default=`, and the insert leaves the column out where it can, or writes `"DEFAULT"` or the default's expression (`django/db/models/sql/compiler.py:SQLInsertCompiler.as_sql`, `django/db/models/expressions.py:DatabaseDefault`).
`GeneratedField` (5.0) is a column the database computes from others in its row, and no save writes it (`django/db/models/fields/generated.py:GeneratedField`).
On MySQL, and on MariaDB for an update, `Model._assign_returned_values` removes the attribute, so that the next read fetches it (`django/db/models/base.py:Model._assign_returned_values`).

Since 6.1 Django makes virtual generated columns on PostgreSQL 18 and stored ones on Oracle 23.7, each having had only the other kind: `GeneratedField.db_persist` chooses, and a check refuses the kind a database lacks (`django/db/models/fields/generated.py:GeneratedField._check_persistence`).
Since 5.2 a constraint's validation handles a generated field, taking it as its expression over the instance's values (`django/db/models/base.py:Model._get_field_expression_map`).

Before 6.1 every `on_delete` was a Python function, which the `Collector` calls for each relation it follows, so that a cascade or a null set was Django's own work (`django/db/models/deletion.py:CASCADE`).

Each is a `DatabaseOnDelete`, which stands with `DO_NOTHING` in `SKIP_COLLECTION`, so the collector that a delete makes does not follow the relation, fetches none of the rows the database removes, and sends them no signal (`django/db/models/deletion.py:DatabaseOnDelete`).

The checks refuse `DB_SET_NULL` on a field that cannot be null, `DB_SET_DEFAULT` on one without `db_default=`, and a chain of references that mixes the database's actions with Python's (`django/db/models/fields/related.py:ForeignKey._check_on_delete`).

`CompositePrimaryKey` (5.2) is a field with no column, assigned to `"pk"`, that names the fields making up the key; its value is a tuple of theirs (`django/db/models/fields/composite.py:CompositePrimaryKey`).

Also in 6.0, `Model._check_local_fields` began to refuse, as `"models.E049"`, a `ForeignObject` with several `from_fields=` named in `"indexes"`, `"constraints"` or `"unique_together"` (`django/db/models/base.py:Model._check_local_fields`).

`Model._is_pk_set` says whether a key is set: not when it is `None`, not when a part of a tuple is, and since 6.1 not when it is the `DatabaseDefault` of a key the database will supply (`django/db/models/base.py:Model._is_pk_set`).
`DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD` has been `"django.db.models.BigAutoField"` by default since 6.0, where it was `"django.db.models.AutoField"` (`django/conf/global_settings.py`).

`Options._get_default_pk_class` picks the class of the `"id"` a model with no primary key is given: that one, unless the application's `AppConfig.default_auto_field` names another (`django/db/models/options.py:Options._get_default_pk_class`).

A project that set neither now gets 64-bit keys, and the autodetector, comparing a key made under the old default with the model, makes an `AlterField` for it (`django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields`).

The setter of `Field.choices` passes the value to `normalize_choices`, which makes the list of pairs and wraps a callable in a `CallableChoiceIterator`, called each time the choices are read (`django/utils/choices.py:normalize_choices`, `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.choices`).

The setter of `Field.choices` passes the value to `normalize_choices`, which makes the list of pairs and wraps a callable in a `CallableChoiceIterator`, called each time the choices are read (`django/utils/choices.py:normalize_choices`, `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.choices`).

Since 6.0 a save told to update, by `force_update=True` or `update_fields=`, that matches no row raises the model's `Model.NotUpdated` in place of a plain `DatabaseError` (`django/db/models/base.py:Model._save_table`; [Saving an instance](../models/saving.md)).

Its comment gives the second base as backward compatibility, an `except` clause not consulting `__subclasshook__`, so code that catches `DatabaseError` still catches it (`django/db/models/base.py:ModelBase.__new__`; [`ModelBase`: a class statement becomes a model](../models/metaclass.md)).
`CheckConstraint` has taken its condition as `condition=` since 5.1, which deprecated `check=`, removed in 6.0 (`django/db/models/constraints.py:CheckConstraint.__init__`).

Since 6.0 `BaseConstraint.check` returns the system check's messages for a model and a connection, and `Model._check_constraints` calls it for each database that may hold the model (`django/db/models/base.py:Model._check_constraints`).
Giving the name or the message by position, deprecated in 5.0, is refused since 6.0 (`django/db/models/constraints.py:BaseConstraint.__init__`).
Now a message given is used, with the code given (`django/db/models/constraints.py:UniqueConstraint.validate`).
`Options.contribute_to_class` refuses it with a `TypeError`, and an `Index` in `"indexes"` takes its place (`django/db/models/options.py:Options.contribute_to_class`).
`AlterIndexTogether` stays, so that old migrations still apply (`django/db/migrations/operations/models.py:AlterIndexTogether`).
